hero.title: Reuse without regret
intro.0: Can't you just inherit everything - one class borrowing from another, and that one borrowing again? It often feels like the natural way to reuse code, and sometimes it is. But inheritance is a strong promise, and forcing it where it does not fit tends to make code harder to change later.
intro.1: Here you build both ways yourself - a type that borrows from a parent, and a type made of smaller parts it holds - meet the reason C# lets a class have only one parent, and see the shared payoff both unlock. So you can pick the right one each time.
task.1.title: A child that is-a parent
task.1.context:
[[concept:pr-inheritance|Inheritance]] reuses code by kinship. Write `class Dog : Animal` and the colon reads 'is a': a `Dog` is a kind of `Animal`, so every `Animal` member comes along for free, and the child adds its own on top.

The pattern below gives a `Car` everything a `Vehicle` has, then adds one method. Do the same for the dog.
task.1.goal.0: Make `Dog` inherit `Animal` so it gets `Breathe()` for free, then add a `Fetch()` that prints `fetches the stick`.
task.1.goal.1: `rex` breathes then fetches, so the output is two lines: ...breathe... then fetches the stick.
task.2.title: An object that has-a part
task.2.context:
[[concept:pr-composition|Composition]] reuses code the other way: instead of being a kind of something, a class holds one and asks it to do the work. No colon, no parent - just a field it owns. Forwarding the call to that held part is called [[concept:pr-delegation|delegation]].

The pattern below gives a `Printer` an `Ink` it holds and delegates to. Do the same: give `Dog` a `Voice`.
task.2.goal.0: Give `Dog` a `Voice` field it owns (a has-a), then make `Bark()` return what the voice says - do not inherit.
task.2.goal.1: The voice says Woof, so `Bark()` returns Woof.
task.3.title: One call, many answers
task.3.context:
Inheritance and composition both build types; [[concept:pr-polymorphism|polymorphism]] is the payoff they unlock. A base type declares a `virtual` method with a default, and each child can `override` it. Hold children in a base-typed array and one call adapts to each real object - no `if` per type.

The base `Animal` and one child (`Dog`) are done. Add `Cat` and `Cow` the same way.
task.3.goal.0: Add `Cat` and `Cow`, each inheriting `Animal` and overriding `Speak()` to return Meow and Moo.
task.3.goal.1: The loop prints each animal's word in array order: Woof, Meow, Moo.
task.4.title: Two abilities, no diamond
task.4.context:
Why favour composition? Imagine a `Duck` that should both swim and fly. With inheritance you would want two parents - `class Duck : Swimmer, Flyer` - but C# forbids it: if both parents offered the same method, the call would be ambiguous. That clash is the diamond problem, and it is the strongest everyday reason to reach for composition.

Composition dissolves it: hold each behaviour as its own part and name it when you delegate. The pattern below mixes two parts; give `Duck` its two.
task.4.goal.0: Give `Duck` a `Swimming` field and a `Flying` field it holds, then delegate `Swim()` to one and `Fly()` to the other - no inheritance.
task.5.title: Reuse without regret recap
task.5.summaryIntro: Two ways to reuse code, and the payoff both unlock:
task.5.summaryItems.0.title: is-a - inheritance
task.5.summaryItems.0.text: a child borrows a parent's members and must be usable as that parent, everywhere.
task.5.summaryItems.1.title: has-a - composition
task.5.summaryItems.1.text: a class holds smaller parts and delegates to them - mix as many as you like.
task.5.summaryItems.2.title: polymorphism
task.5.summaryItems.2.text: one call over a base type adapts to each real object, so there is no if per type.
task.5.summaryItems.3.title: favour composition
task.5.summaryItems.3.text: inheritance allows one parent and can force a bad fit; held parts never clash - that is why we lean on composition.
task.5.summaryClose: The keeper rule: can you honestly say A is-a B, always and everywhere? If not - or if you need to mix behaviours - hold parts instead. You will lean on this again when you design bigger systems: the same has-a move lets you swap one part for another without disturbing the rest.
concept.pr-inheritance.def: Reuse by claiming kinship - a child class is-a kind of its parent and gets the parent's members for free.
concept.pr-composition.def: Reuse by holding parts - a class has-a smaller object as a field and asks it to do the work.
concept.pr-polymorphism.def: One call that adapts to the real object behind it, so the same method name gives many behaviours.
concept.pr-favour-composition.def: Preferring has-a parts over deep inheritance, since inheritance can force a bad fit and multiple parents clash.
